entry.title: Australian Rail, Tram and Bus Industry Union (139V) v Metro Trains Melbourne Pty Ltd Trading AS Metro Trains Melbourne [2026] FWC 4209
entry.content:
The RTBU brought a s 739 dispute alleging that Metro Trains’ CCTV Operators were misclassified as Authorised Officer Level 3 (ODE) and should be reclassified under Schedule D of the enterprise agreement. The Commission rejected Metro’s jurisdictional objections and found the current classification inappropriate, selecting Operational Support Officer (ODF) as the best comparator.

Key holding: An enterprise agreement clause granting employees a role-review right during the agreement’s life is enforceable independently of a separate aspirational process for finalising classification descriptors.

Clause 3.15.1 confers an explicit, unconditional right on all Part 3 employees to apply for a review of their roles and responsibilities "during the life of the agreement" . There is nothing linking clause 3.15.1 to clause E.3.1.

entry.title: Mr Steven Kitching v Woodham Petroleum Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4237
entry.content:
This was an application by Woodham Petroleum Pty Ltd to dismiss Mr Kitching’s unfair dismissal application under s 399A of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). Mr Kitching had repeatedly failed to attend FWC conferences and failed to file material in accordance with directions despite warnings. The Commission dismissed the unfair dismissal application.

Key holding: The FWC may dismiss an unfair dismissal application where the applicant unreasonably fails to attend FWC conferences and comply with FWC directions, after being given opportunities and warnings.

After considering all circumstances in this matter, I am satisfied that Mr Kitching has unreasonably failed to attend conferences and comply with directions relating to his application. In these circumstances, it is appropriate to dismiss his application.

entry.content:

The application was filed 56 days outside the 21-day period, and the Fair Work Commission dismissed it because no exceptional circumstances justified an extension of time.

Key holding: Ignorance of the statutory time limit will not ordinarily weigh in favour of a finding of exceptional circumstances for extending time.

It is well established that ignorance of the statutory time period, in the analogous circumstances of late unfair dismissal applications, does not weigh in favour of a finding of exceptional circumstances.

entry.title: Application by "Automotive, Food, Metals, Engineering, Printing and Kindred Industries Union" known as the Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union (AMWU) (188V) [2026] FWC 4234
entry.content:

entry.title: The Australasian Meat Industry Employees Union (007V) v Bindaree Beef Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4228
entry.content:
The AMIEU applied under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for the Fair Work Commission to deal with a dispute over employees stood down without pay on 16 and 19 June 2026. Bindaree Beef objected that the AMIEU had not completed the mandatory dispute-resolution steps in cl 41 of the enterprise agreement before referring the dispute to the Commission. The Commission dismissed the proceedings for want of jurisdiction.

Key holding: Where an enterprise agreement makes completion of each dispute-resolution step mandatory, the Commission lacks jurisdiction under s 739 unless those steps, including any final internal referral, have been completed before referral to the FWC.

For the reasons I have set out, the step in clause 41.3(d) of the Agreement cannot be said to have been "completed" as required by clause 41.3(e). It follows that the condition precedent to the AMIEU being able to refer the matter to the Commission was not met.

entry.title: Mrs Julie Bray v Crowther Pitt Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4244
entry.content:
In Bray v Crowther Pitt Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4244, the Fair Work Commission considered whether Ms Bray’s dismissal from an early learning centre was a genuine redundancy under s 389 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). Crowther Pitt had abolished her administrative role and offered an educator position, which Ms Bray declined. The Commission upheld the employer’s jurisdictional objection and dismissed the unfair dismissal application.

Key holding: A dismissal is not unfair where the employer establishes all three elements of genuine redundancy under s 389, because the dismissal then falls outside the unfair dismissal definition in s 385.

Given my three findings above, Ms Bray's dismissal was a case of "genuine redundancy" as defined in s.389 of the FW Act. That means Ms Bray cannot satisfy the definition of an unfair dismissal in s.385 of the FW Act.

entry.title: Mr Timothy Read v SRG Global Assets Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4240
entry.content:
This was an unfair dismissal application by Mr Timothy Read against SRG Global Assets Pty Ltd after his employment was terminated while he was on long-term medical leave following hip surgery. The Fair Work Commission found the dismissal harsh and unreasonable because the employer lacked a valid capacity-based reason and denied procedural fairness. The matter has been listed for further directions on remedy.

Key holding: A dismissal for long-term incapacity will be unreasonable where it is not supported by a valid reason and is affected by a denial of procedural fairness.

The dismissal was harsh and unreasonable. It was harsh in the context of the Applicant's personal circumstances, and unreasonable given the absence of a valid reason and denial of procedural fairness.

entry.content:

Commissioner Connolly was satisfied, on balance, that Mr Montebello is a fit and proper person after considering the s.513(1) permit qualification matters and supporting declarations.

Key holding: Whether an official is a fit and proper person to hold an entry permit is assessed at the time of determination by reference to the s.513(1) permit qualification matters and the powers, functions and responsibilities attached to holding a permit, rather than in the abstract.

The focus of the Commission's inquiry is not whether the proposed permit holder is a fit and proper person in some abstract sense. entry.title: Linh Tran v Westpac Banking Corporation trading as Bank of Melbourne [2026] FWCFB 287
entry.content:
Linh Tran appealed a Fair Work Commission decision dismissing his s 739 application concerning redeployment and redundancy entitlements under the Westpac Group Enterprise Agreement 2023. The Full Bench granted permission to appeal and found the Commissioner erred on compliance with steps 1–3 of the dispute procedure, but dismissed the appeal because Mr Tran had not maintained the dispute after the Bank’s final response and could not refer it in perpetuity.

Key holding: Absent an express time limit, an enterprise agreement dispute clause does not allow a party to refer a dispute to the Commission under step 4 in perpetuity.

While it was not a feature of the 2023 Agreement that applications to the Commission were to be made within an express time limit, we do not consider it follows that it remained open to a party to refer a dispute to the Commission under step 4 in perpetuity.

entry.title: Mrs Carolyn Monks v The Hobart Clinic Association Limited Trading AS The Hobart Clinic [2026] FWCFB 288
entry.content:
Mrs Monks lodged a s 365 general protections application after already making an unfair dismissal application that remained on foot. The Full Bench refused permission to appeal from the Deputy President’s decision dismissing the s 365 application as contrary to s 725 of the Fair Work Act 2009.

Key holding: A s 365 general protections application is barred by s 725 where an earlier unfair dismissal application in relation to the same dismissal has not been withdrawn and has not failed for want of jurisdiction or genuine redundancy.

Even within the confines of an application for permission to appeal, which is concerned to identify arguable error and not to determine the merits of the appeal, it is clear that Mrs Monks' general protections claim was barred by s 725.

entry.content:

Key holding: In determining whether a parent poses an unacceptable risk of future harm, a court may rely on findings about past conduct and present insight as the foundation for the predictive assessment.

entry.title: FDB17 v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1612
entry.content:
The appellant, a Pakistani protection visa applicant, appealed a Federal Circuit and Family Court judgment dismissing his judicial review application concerning an AAT decision that affirmed refusal of his visa. He argued the Tribunal fell into jurisdictional error by unreasonably declining to telephone four corroborating witnesses (his parents, brother and a friend) who had already provided a joint signed statement. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal, holding the Tribunal's approach had a rational and intelligible foundation.

Key holding: Where a decision-maker is convinced that an applicant's account is fabricated or fundamentally unreliable, it is not irrational or illogical to decline to hear oral corroborating evidence and to reject that corroboration, even absent any independent ground for doubting the corroborators.

It is not necessarily irrational, or illogical, for a finder of fact, who is convinced that a principal witness is fabricating a story, which is considered to be inherently implausible, to reject corroborative evidence, even though there is no separate or independent ground for its rejection, apart from the reasons given for disbelieving the principal witness.

entry.title: Mr Stephen Morgan v Origin Education Group Pty Ltd Trading AS Origin Institute [2026] FWC 4222
entry.content:
Stephen Morgan applied for unfair dismissal under s.394 after his casual vocational trainer engagement with Origin Institute ended. The employer objected that he had not served the minimum employment period because his casual work was not regular and systematic and he lacked a reasonable expectation of continuing employment. The Fair Work Commission found the jurisdictional objection failed and Mr Morgan was protected from unfair dismissal.

Key holding: Casual employment can be systematic under s 384(2)(a)(i) and s 12 where it is arranged according to an identifiable system, even if the hours or availability are unpredictable.

Adopting the test from Chandler at [18]: the employment need only be arranged pursuant to an identifiable system for it to be on a systematic basis.

entry.title: Mark Thomas v ABC Photosigns Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4205
entry.content:

Key holding: An extension under s 366(2) requires the Commission to be satisfied, after considering all statutory factors individually and together, that exceptional circumstances exist; satisfaction cannot be reached where the applicant provides no acceptable explanation for the delay even if some other factors favour an extension.

Having considered each of the factors in s 366(2) individually and together, I am not satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances to extend time in this matter.

The AMWU applied under s 437 of the Fair Work Act 2009 for a protected action ballot order for Sims Limited employees. Sims opposed the application as premature and said the AMWU was not genuinely trying to reach agreement, also raising ballot-question clarity and safety concerns. The Commission granted the application, allowed a typographical amendment, and issued a PABO with a non-AEC ballot agent.

Key holding: An application for a protected action ballot order is not premature merely because bargaining has not been exhausted or reached a particular stage; s 443(1)(b) requires an assessment of whether the applicant has been and is genuinely trying to reach agreement.

However, for reasons set out above, under the Act there is no requirement that the bargaining be exhausted before an application of this kind is made. Further, a PABO application or order does not stop the bargaining and the good faith bargaining obligations remain, including that the parties must continue to bargain.

entry.title: Rangel & Bird (No 2) [2026] FedCFamC1A 193
entry.content:
This was a mother’s appeal against three parenting orders concerning the children’s international travel, passports and extra-curricular activities. The appellate court found the primary judge denied procedural fairness by making orders materially outside the case presented by the parties and the Independent Children’s Lawyer. The appeal was allowed, the relevant orders were set aside, and the discretion was re-exercised.

entry.title: Fred-Tutavaha v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1586
entry.content:
The applicant, a New Zealand citizen who arrived in Australia aged four, sought judicial review of the Assistant Minister's decision under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to set aside an AAT decision revoking the cancellation of his visa. He ran three grounds — unreasonable delay, failure to consider immigration detention as a legal consequence, and legal unreasonableness in giving legal consequences "neutral weight" — with the Court also considering a proposed fourth ground on the national interest assessment.

Key holding: A failure to refer expressly to immigration detention in reasons for a s 501BA cancellation does not permit an inference that this legal consequence was not considered, where detention pending removal is an obvious and well-known statutory consequence and there is no barrier to removal.

It does not follow, however, that the proper inference is that the Assistant Minister failed to appreciate that a legal consequence of his decision was that the Applicant would be taken into immigration detention. The statement of reasons must be read fairly and as a whole, and the fact that a matter is not mentioned expressly does not necessarily mean it was not considered
